v.q: Which interface has exactly one abstract method and can therefore be the target of a lambda?
o: Any interface with default methods only
Any abstract class with one method
v.w: The rule is one abstract method. Default and static methods, and re-declared `Object` methods, do not count.

v.q: Which interface can NOT be the target of a lambda?
o: An interface with two abstract methods
A custom interface with one abstract method
v.w: A lambda needs exactly one abstract method. Default and static methods do not count.

v.q: Which functional interface takes no argument and returns a value?
v.w: Supplier: `() -> T`. Consumer: `T -> void`. Predicate: `T -> boolean`. Function: `T -> R`.

v.q: Which functional interface takes one argument and returns a boolean?
v.w: Predicate tests a value. Consumer returns nothing and Supplier takes no argument.

v.q: What does this code do? `int count = 0; list.forEach(x -> count++);`
o: It does not compile: captured locals must be effectively final
It counts the elements of the list correctly
It counts correctly, but only on one thread
It throws an exception when the lambda runs
v.w: A lambda captures a copy of the value, so the local cannot change. Use `list.size()`, `stream().count()` or an `AtomicInteger`.

v.q: Which rewrite counts list elements correctly?
o: A lambda that increments a local int
A lambda that increments a final int
A lambda that assigns a captured local
v.w: Captured locals must be effectively final. For a count, use size(), count() or an AtomicInteger.

v.q: What does `this` refer to inside a lambda body?
o: The enclosing object, as in the surrounding method
v.w: An anonymous inner class has its own `this`. A lambda does not introduce a new scope for `this`.

v.q: Which statement about this inside a lambda is NOT true?
o: It refers to the lambda object
It refers to the enclosing object
It behaves like this in the surrounding method
It differs from an anonymous class
v.w: An anonymous class has its own this. A lambda does not.

v.q: What is the difference between `orElse(x)` and `orElseGet(supplier)` on an `Optional`?
o: `orElse` always evaluates `x`, `orElseGet` calls the supplier only when empty
`orElseGet` always evaluates its argument, `orElse` does not
They are identical, only the names differ
v.w: With `orElse(createDefault())` the default is built even when a value is present. Prefer `orElseGet` for anything expensive.

v.q: Why is orElse(createDefault()) a risk when createDefault is expensive?
o: It runs even when a value is present
It throws if the value exists
v.w: The argument is evaluated before the call. orElseGet takes a supplier that runs only when needed.

o: As the return type of a method that may find nothing
As a field type in a JPA entity
As a method parameter that callers may skip
As the element type of a `List`
v.w: It was designed for return values. For fields and parameters use plain types, overloads or validation; for no results, return an empty collection.

v.q: Which use of Optional is NOT recommended?
o: A field of a JPA entity
The return type of a finder method
A return value that may be absent
v.w: Optional is meant for return values. As a field or parameter it adds noise and is not serializable.

v.q: `find(id).map(this::findBranch)` where `findBranch` itself returns an `Optional<Branch>`. What type results, and what is the better call?
v.w: `map` wraps the function's result. `flatMap` expects the function to return an `Optional` and does not wrap it again.

v.q: What does flatMap do on an Optional whose function returns an Optional?
o: Returns a single Optional without nesting
Throws when the inner is empty
v.w: flatMap flattens, so the result is one Optional. map would nest them.

v.q: How is `Predicate<Account> p = a -> a.isActive();` best combined with another predicate `q`?
v.w: `Predicate` has `and`, `or` and `negate`. `Function` has `andThen` and `compose`. Compose small named pieces instead of one long lambda.
Predicate has and, or and negate. Predicate.not(p) is the static form.
